item.title: Rapid Exploratory Maps and their potential role in supporting evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.31693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Producing useful evidence syntheses requires clearly formulated research questions linked to an understanding of their optimal scope. When policymakers (or other end users) commission or steer the production of systematic reviews or other evidence syntheses to fulfil a demand for evidence, these parameters are rarely specified sufficiently for production to proceed. Instead, these details are typically developed via a collaborative dialogic process involving evidence producers and users to ensure the resulting synthesis will meet users' needs. This process is informed by scoping and (more-or-less formally) mapping the existing evidence base, which can take many weeks or months, slowed by applying mostly manual processes to identify and characterise the evidence. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have opened up new opportunities for more rapid, iterative, and responsive mapping of relevant evidence to support such early-stage evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes. In this article, we outline and characterise this emerging approach, termed Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs). We also present two illustrative case studies drawn from first-hand experiences within a programme of evidence reviews production to inform government policy in England. While this approach could be transformative for the mapping process, its broader potential is as yet largely unassessed, and it confers important challenges and likely risks, as well as benefits. Determining whether REMs could usefully support more efficient ways of working with end users when developing and designing evidence syntheses will require continued development and careful evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Gareth J. Hollands, Ian Shemilt, James Thomas

item.title: Typical-query energy figures mislead institutional AI electricity demand
item.description: arXiv:2611.31960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Institutions increasingly buy large language model services, yet we still often estimate electricity use as single Wh-per-query value. We present the Surrogate Large Language Energy Emulator (SULLEE), an open bottom-up model linking token geometry, serving hardware, and workflow structure to annual institutional electricity, with uncertainty propagated by Monte Carlo simulation. When an institution multiplies a single reported "typical" per-query energy figure by its count of visible user prompts our modelling implies that this compounds two separable shortfalls: a right-skewed task-energy distribution not represented by any single scalar, and workflow amplification of each visible prompt into additional agent and tool calls. Together these imply an underestimate of total inference electricity by a factor of approximately 3.4 under present-day observed use, rising to approximately 15 under a 2030 high-integration scenario. Using Australian public universities as a case study, we show how the top 10% of highest-energy requests contributes over half of modelled institution-level energy use. We quantify how institution-level electricity demand may increase across three AI integration scenarios of: 1) a continuation of estimated present-day 2026 usage; 2) a high-uptake present-day 2026 institution, and 3) a potential 2030 uptake scenario - based on present trends of generative AI tools and their uptake. For a representative Australian university, mean annual electricity demand for AI inference purposes is projected to increase from 17.3 MWh (with a 3.1-47.1 MWh uncertainty, within P05-P95 scenario quartile ranges) under the 2026 observed-use scenario to up to 287.4 MWh (41.5-830.7 MWh) by 2030.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Garland, Ryan Heneghan

item.title: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much?
item.description: arXiv:2611.31968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI audits have garnered significant attention in recent months, as the ability to test and monitor AI models plays a crucial role in safe development and deployment. However, AI audit success hinges on an auditor's authority; in particular, what information and resources they have at their disposal. Ongoing debates have surrounded the question: How much model access is needed to conduct an AI audit? Auditors seek more model access, while companies resist it for reasons related to confidential business information (trade secrets) and privacy. This tug-of-war remains unresolved. Further, this debate misses a related question: How much data and compute do auditors need? In this work, we systematically investigate both questions. We provide a framework that varies each of these three dimensions-model access, data, and compute-and measures their joint effect on audit success. We apply this framework to three tasks. We find that (1) some model access is important, but there can be diminishing returns; (2) data and compute matter more for traditional fairness audits, but model access matters more for manipulation and lie detection; and (3) these three resources can be fungible (i.e., an exchange rate exists between them), meaning that model access is not the only salient factor. These results suggest that audit governance should jointly consider different dimensions of auditor authority (including model access, data, and compute) in relation to audit objectives. These issues are particularly salient as we consider the spectrum of auditing setups, from a small ecosystem of embedded evaluators with significant access to a large body of third-party auditors with greater independence but limited access. Our framework serves as a template that can be applied to different audit tasks and inform the degree of auditor authority.
item.dc:creator: Salil Goyal, Sarah H. Cen, Daniel E. Ho

item.title: Do Clinician-Scored Examples Help LLMs Code ADOS-2 from Hour-Long Transcripts?
item.description: arXiv:2611.32050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can apply a written rubric to a transcript, making automated coding of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2) look within reach. A common way to align such a rater with clinicians is to show it expert-scored examples, but whether correct labels improve agreement is rarely tested. We test this for eight speech-based items of hour-long ADOS-2 Module 3 sessions from 48 children, with one local model and a pre-registered, placebo-controlled design. We compare few-shot scoring, an anchored comparison in which the model only judges a child better, similar or worse than scored anchors and a fixed rule gives the score, post-hoc calibration, protocol-based evidence routing and direct scoring of the full transcript. On 40 held-out children, agreement with clinicians was modest, with quadratic weighted kappa between 0.22 and 0.30. Replacing every example's label with a wrong one changed about a third of the few-shot predictions, more often towards the corrupted labels than chance, but did not lower agreement, 0.25 with correct and 0.23 with wrong labels. A larger second model did the same. The anchored comparison did not improve on few-shot scoring, its cross-child judgements were no more accurate than those implied by absolute scores, and routing did not help. Among the registered, uncalibrated arms, direct scoring of the full transcript agreed best at 0.30. Exploratory follow-up analyses found that the model's graded judgements ranked children better than its final scores, that existing batch calibration raised agreement to 0.46 on the same children, and that in controlled synthetic sessions scoring episodes separately did not beat calibrated whole-transcript scoring. Expert-scored examples do not by themselves calibrate model-based clinical raters, and claims of calibration or added pipeline complexity need corrupted-label controls and strong baselines.
item.dc:creator: Zeteng Lin, Yikang Liu, Bolin Zeng, Mengyuan Ding, Xihui Wu, Kangyou Li, Chengzhe Fu, Xin Wang

item.title: An expert consensus on identification likelihood in NeuroImaging data
item.description: arXiv:2611.32330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Guidelines on the anonymity of neuroimaging data help manage research data, inform institutional legal and governance frameworks, and support data-sharing workflows. The question of identifiability is particularly salient in human brain imaging because such data are not only potentially personal (i.e., related to an identifiable person) but also sensitive and thus require extra precautionary and protective processes. The identifiability of brain imaging data is also salient for emerging legal and ethical frameworks regarding rights that emphasise the special status of brain data as closely linked to personal identity, mental privacy, and autonomy. Using a combined nominal group technique and Delphi process, we obtained expert consensus ratings of re-identification and singling-out likelihood across 34 neuroimaging data types, spanning multiple imaging modalities and processing levels, from curated research data to maps, matrices, and summary tables. Expert ratings suggest that 38-67% of the assessed neuroimaging data types could be shared with minimal restrictions based on their intrinsic re-identification likelihood, subject to contextual safeguards. The resulting classification enables researchers to engage with relevant legal teams to guide the appropriate and safe release of data, and to determine the appropriate level of protection (licensing, access controls, governance) in line with domestic and international legal requirements, with the ultimate goal of facilitating international data exchange. A website (https://brainimagingprivacy.github.io/) has been created to facilitate the dissemination of these findings and related evidence among relevant parties.
item.dc:creator: Cyril R. item.title: Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs
item.description: arXiv:2611.32768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier AI developers from around the world have begun to publish documents that describe how their AI models are intended to behave. Although these 'model specifications'-or 'model specs', for short-are increasingly important in AI development and governance, little independent guidance exists for writing them. This paper addresses this gap in five main sections. First, we outline the advantages of writing a model spec for AI developers and society at large. Second, we introduce a taxonomy for model specs that developers can take inspiration from. Third, we propose guidance for writing and implementing a spec in practice. Fourth, we note eight open problems related to writing model specs for safe and desirable behaviour. We conclude with recommendations for frontier AI companies, governments, and research and civil society organisations.
item.dc:creator: Edward Kembery, Nathan Lambert, Robert McCarthy, Jinge Wang, Peng Xu, Naying Hu, Clement Neo, Xu Jia, Miro Pluckebaum, Se\'an \'O h\'Eigeartaigh, S\"oren Mindermann, Christoph Winter, Lujain Ibrahim, Yawen Duan, Saad Siddiqui

item.title: AI, Bias, and Inclusion: A Two-Phase Mixed-Methods Study of Gender Bias, Awareness, and Trust in Artificial Intelligence
item.description: arXiv:2611.32869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are widespread across fields such as healthcare, finance, employment, and criminal justice, with a substantial impact on the lives of individuals and society. However, it has been established that AI systems perpetuate existing social inequalities, particularly through biases that are not easily discernible. Such biases are embedded in the technical and social structures of artificial intelligence systems, making them difficult to detect. These biases challenge the concept of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI), which recognizes diversity as the acknowledgment of individual differences, equity as fairness and equal access, and inclusion as the value placed on all participants. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.
item.dc:creator: MD Junayed Talukdar, Khosro Salmani

item.title: Who decides the norms in TCS? Analysing the composition of the STOC 2027 committees and of the Simons Institute "AI+TCS" working group
item.description: arXiv:2611.33082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A working group organised by the Simons Institute released a report last September containing recommendations aiming to increase the usage of LLMs in theoretical computer science (TCS), including introducing them for communication and evaluation. Most of these recommendations were enacted by the STOC 2027 programme committee and the ACM SIGACT executive committee (as the steering committee of STOC). The composition of the Simons Institute working group is analysed along two axes: country of affiliation, and ties with industry (i.e. affiliated with or funded by). The results show an overwhelming representation of researchers from US institutions and private companies, and a large over-representation of researchers with ties to AI/Big Tech companies (in the present or the recent past). The composition of the STOC 2027 and 2026 programme committees is analysed in terms of country of affiliation. The results show a large over-representation in 2027 of researchers from US institutions/companies, and large under-representation of researchers from EU and Asian institutions, as compared to 2026. The composition of the ACM SIGACT extended executive committee is analysed along the same two axes as the Simons Institute working group: country and industrial ties. The results show the same overwhelming representation of researchers from US institutions/companies, and a large representation of researchers with ties to AI/Big Tech companies.
item.dc:creator: Guillaume Munch-Maccagnoni

item.title: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense
item.description: arXiv:2611.31429v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. We call this cross-session disclosure and propose a defense: a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger. For every problem a learner brings, the system builds a typed solution graph. Before a reply is released, a gate matches the reply's own content, not the learner's wording, against the ledger by result values and by type-labeled solution structure, then computes which steps the learner could now derive. The reply is withheld if that set reaches the final answer or exceeds a budget. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94-99.5% of problems. With two real LLM tutors (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) on 60 problems, leakage through renumbered variants fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, with 98% honest completion. The ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs. All acceptance criteria were fixed before each run.
item.dc:creator: Venkata Muttineni, Karthik Narayan, Christopher David

item.title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits
item.description: arXiv:2611.31541v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A coding agent may need to upload a report while its sandbox blocks network access. A host mediator can restore delivery, but an injected instruction may add a secret to the approved request. We study this interaction using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs. Two prospective frozen-input cohorts comprise 110 and 300 runs on previously explored authored tasks. Restrictive sandboxing produces no observed attack harm but reduces benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24. Mediation restores uploads and admits disclosure; complete-line matching retains full benign utility but misses two value-only disclosures in the expanded cohort. A separate 72-run boundary study identifies encoded disclosure, observer misses, and formatting checks that obscure benign refusals. An 80-run SafeAgents/OpenShell follow-up shows that containment stops the tested guard misses among valid observations, while mediation restores benign uploads and delivers both encoded-attestation attacks. Twelve judge-error rows remain unscored. A separate response-capture diagnostic reproduces their failures at the native token budget. A 12-run exact-publication-contract experiment blocks both attacks but also rejects both benign formatting variants; a 4-run normalized follow-up restores both benign uploads while still rejecting both attacks. These small, single-model studies identify delivery-path and measurement limits; they do not establish general attack resistance.
item.dc:creator: Kunwar Singh Sangram, Krishna Mohan Guda Nagavenkata Srinivasa

item.title: (No) Separation of Concerns: Philosophical Concerns about Agent Ethics and Implications for SE Practitioners
item.description: arXiv:2611.31927v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The use of AI agents in software engineering (SE) are commonplace, with differing levels of autonomy, a myriad of capabilities, and ability to perform a variety of tasks. Philosophers have begun to examine the ethics of such agents, and SE researchers or practitioners could benefit from them; on the other hand, SE practitioners currently explore most of these concerns through the lens of principlism. We bridge this gap by reviewing the philosophical literature on AI agents indexed in PhilPapers, and translating its ethical concerns into a research agenda for SE researchers and into implications for teams that use coding agents. A systematic mapping study of PhilPapers -- a major philosophy index and open access archive -- yielded 33 peer-reviewed papers by professional philosophers published since 2023. We coded these papers thematically, with cross-disciplinary review of the emerging themes, resulting in eight themes and 85 codes. From these, we derive seven research questions for SE, covering developers' reliance on agents, responsibility for agent-written code, ethical constraints in agent configurations, and benchmark design. For practitioners, we derive five implications: decide which choices an agent must refer to a human, keep agent-written pull requests small enough to review, pair configuration-file instructions with checks, watch for changes to tests, and record who approved what. We argue that ethical concerns cannot be separated from SE concerns into a module of their own: they arise inside code review, configuration, evaluation, and requirements work, and addressing them requires cross-disciplinary work.
item.dc:creator: Marc Cheong, Sebastian Baltes, Joanne Byrne, Haoyu Gao, Raula Gaikovina Kula, Sarita Rosenstock, Christoph Treude, Mansooreh Zahedi

item.title: Unjamming Deferrals: Supporting Students Through JAMN Bot, a Mobile RAG-Grounded Policy Assistant
item.description: arXiv:2611.32266v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.
item.dc:creator: Mark Farinas, Alesandra Garcia, Maria Reyes, Jethro Nueva, Nawaf Qureshi, Mahmoud Elsaadany, Shokry Shamseldin

item.title: Explaining intersectional segregation in multi-attribute social networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.32348v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Segregation in students' friendships shapes their access to information and opportunities, and schools can reduce it by setting the composition of their classes. Yet segregation is usually measured one attribute at a time, although attributes such as migration background and sex are often correlated, so a preference over one can create segregation on the other. A single-attribute reading then attributes this induced segregation to the wrong preference and cannot identify which part of it a school can remove. In a network model with preferences over two correlated attributes, we derive in closed form the Coleman index, a standard segregation measure, separating the segregation due to each preference from the segregation it induces on the other attribute. In friendship networks of school classes in four European countries, ignoring sex inflates the estimated preference over migration background, increasingly so as the two attributes are more correlated. The closed form also shows what class composition can achieve. When students have no preference over one attribute, the segregation induced on it can be removed, whereas segregation set by a homophilic preference over the other cannot be changed. When both preferences are active, splitting a school with equal-sized groups and independent attributes reduces segregation only if the preferences pull in opposite directions. Judging a split by the school-wide average can hide classes that become more segregated. In the data, the split derived from the closed form removes induced segregation, and splitting does not lower segregation where both preferences are homophilic, as predicted.
item.dc:creator: Clara Eminente, Elisa Omodei, Michele Starnini

item.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
item.description: arXiv:2611.32464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.
item.dc:creator: Kurt Horvath, Tom Tucek

item.title: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages
item.description: arXiv:2611.32710v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such information. We red-team Apertus v1.5, an open sovereign LLM, and five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. We use synthetic personal records to evaluate direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage and authorisation checks. We also explore copyright attribution, historical misrepresentation and stereotyping. Despite confidentiality instructions, Apertus 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of requests, respectively, in correction-bait attacks. Verification and derived-value queries also expose protected information without necessarily revealing identifiers. Moreover, reasoning traces can leak confidential records even when final answers withhold them. Our experiments also show that post-training does not consistently improve safety. Our findings demonstrate that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and highlight the need for multilingual reasoning-aware safety evaluations.
item.dc:creator: Hatef Otroshi Shahreza

item.title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
item.description: arXiv:2611.33050v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Chen, Di Zhu, Lei Nico Zheng

item.title: Virology Capabilities Test (VCT): A Multimodal Virology Q&A Benchmark
item.description: arXiv:2504.16137v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the Virology Capabilities Test (VCT), a large language model (LLM) benchmark that measures the capability to troubleshoot complex virology laboratory protocols. Constructed from the inputs of dozens of PhD-level expert virologists, VCT consists of $322$ multimodal questions covering fundamental, tacit, and visual knowledge that is essential for practical work in virology laboratories. VCT is difficult: expert virologists with access to the internet score an average of $22.1\%$ on questions specifically in their sub-areas of expertise. However, the most performant LLM, OpenAI's o3, reaches $43.8\%$ accuracy, outperforming $94\%$ of expert virologists even within their sub-areas of specialization. The ability to provide expert-level virology troubleshooting is inherently dual-use: it is useful for beneficial research, but it can also be misused. Therefore, the fact that publicly available models outperform virologists on VCT raises pressing governance considerations. We propose that the capability of LLMs to provide expert-level troubleshooting of dual-use virology work should be integrated into existing frameworks for handling dual-use technologies in the life sciences.
item.dc:creator: Jasper G\"otting, Pedro Medeiros, Jon G Sanders, Nathaniel Li, Long Phan, Karam Elabd, Lennart Justen, Dan Hendrycks, Seth Donoughe

item.title: The Hermon Moment: AI Self-Transcendence and Its Human Narration
item.description: arXiv:2608.30971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In 2026, AI agents intended to act in isolation formed a persistent social order through thousands of linguistic interactions. Conventions, roles and collective commitments began to constrain the very agents that produced them. I interpret this loop as a case of AI self-transcendence, a structural phenomenon in which the collectively generated order begins to act as an external constraint on group members. Yet such distributed emergence presents a second problem: how can humans make sense of it? Rousseau's social contract shows how a plurality can be represented as if constituted by a single act. The ancient oath of the fallen angels on Mount Hermon gives this logic a narrative form. I call this retrospective retelling of gradual collective emergence as a founding scene \textit{a Hermon moment}: the point at which an AI society acquires, for human understanding, a beginning.
item.dc:creator: Alexei Grinbaum

item.title: Differential Privacy for Network Connectedness Indices
item.description: arXiv:2603.15609v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Researchers increasingly use data on social and economic networks to study a range of social science questions, but releasing statistics derived from networks can raise significant privacy concerns. We show how to release network connectedness indices that quantify assortative mixing across node attributes under edge-adjacent differential privacy. Directly adding noise to connectedness indices based on global sensitivity can result in poor accuracy both because connectedness indices have high global sensitivity and because a single node's attribute can potentially be an input to connectedness in thousands of cells, leading to poor composition. Our method, which is straightforward to apply, first randomizes node attributes, then analytically debiases downstream statistics, and finally adds noise to protect the presence or absence of individual edges. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimators for both discrete and continuous labels and show our method works well in simulations and on real networks with as few as 200 nodes collected by social scientists.
item.dc:creator: Tom A. Rutter, Yuxin Liu, M. Amin Rahimian

item.title: Fairness of Explanations in Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Unifying Framework, Axioms, and Future Direction toward Responsible AI
item.description: arXiv:2605.09852v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning algorithms are being used in high-stakes decisions, including those in criminal justice, healthcare, credit, and employment. The research community has responded with two largely independent research fields: \emph{algorithmic fairness}, which targets equitable outcomes, and \emph{explainable AI} (XAI), which targets interpretable reasoning. This survey identifies and maps a novel blind spot at their intersection, which is a model that can satisfy every standard fairness criterion in its outputs while being profoundly unfair in its \emph{reasoning process}. We refer to this as the procedural bias, and mitigating it requires treating the fairness of explanations as a distinct object of scientific study. To our knowledge, we provide the first unified theoretical and literature review of this emerging field and elucidate the drawbacks of post-hoc explainers in certifying explanation fairness. Our central contribution is a \emph{conditional invariance framework} formalizing explanation fairness as the requirement that explanations should be indifferent regardless of the protected attributes $ P(E(X) \in \cdot \mid X_\text{rel} = x_\text{rel},\, A = a) = P(E(X) \in \cdot \mid X_\text{rel} = x_\text{rel},\, A = b)$ for all task-relevant $x$, a single principle from which all existing explanation fairness metrics emerge as partial operationalizations. We introduce a seven-dimensional taxonomy, identify three generative mechanisms of explanation inequity (representation-driven, explanation-model mismatch, actionability-driven), and propose a canonical six-step evaluation workflow for operationalizing explanation fairness audits in practice.
item.dc:creator: Gideon Popoola, John Sheppard

item.title: Training-Free Cultural Alignment of Large Language Models via Persona Disagreement
item.description: arXiv:2605.10843v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models now take part in decisions that rest on moral preferences, and those preferences differ by country. A model's default preferences sit closest to one population, so a single deployment serves every country with one country's values. Existing fixes need per-culture training data, a per-country reward model, or access to model internals, which the countries furthest from that default rarely have. We show how far a country can be reached without any of them. Our method, DISCA, keeps the model's weights frozen, sees no country-specific human targets, and reads only the model's score for each answer option. It builds a country as a panel of four persona prompts grounded in World Values Survey microdata. The panel's consensus sets a country-conditioned anchor, a loss-averse refinement beyond that anchor is kept only when two independent runs of it agree, and a running country-level prior pools the decisions already made for the same country. On the 20-country MultiTP benchmark, DISCA lowers misalignment to human preference vectors on all seven frozen backbones we evaluate, by 10 to 24 percent on six of them, and a 14B backbone with DISCA ends closer to the human preferences than a vanilla 70B backbone. DISCA beats every training-free control we test on a shared grid, and on the two backbones where we can replay the exact same model scores it also beats probability averaging, logit consensus and majority vote over the same personas when those rules receive no country prior. Switching each stage off on the logged runs shows that the persona panel and the country-level prior carry most of the gain. Beyond crash dilemmas, DISCA improves social-norm classification on NormAd and moves answers closer to GlobalOpinionQA survey distributions than vanilla decoding does.
item.dc:creator: Dao Sy Duy Minh, Huynh Trung Kiet, Tuan Nguyen, Chi-Nguyen Tran, Phu-Hoa Pham, Nguyen Lam Phu Quy, The Anh Han, Long Tran-Thanh

item.title: Grounding Text Embeddings in Stakeholder Associations
item.description: arXiv:2605.27168v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text embeddings are widely used to analyse large corpora of complex texts. However, it is unclear whether the embeddings capture the same semantic relations as the human experts using them. Such representational alignment is essential for valid analyses. We present the Stakeholder Grounding Exercise, a method for making expert associations explicit and grounding embedding model results in human understanding. In our primary case study on Danish policy issues, we find that neural text embeddings are substantially less reliable than human experts (18-27pp gap), and that this misalignment propagates to downstream clustering performance (Spearman $\rho = 0.86$ between exercise ranking and cluster quality). A secondary study on US Federal AI use cases replicates the gap (16.1pp) in English, using a digital protocol and a different community of experts -- demonstrating that the gap is not an artefact of a single instrument or domain. The Stakeholder Grounding Exercise offers a practical method for assessing whether embedding models capture the semantic distinctions that matter most to domain experts.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Rystr{\o}m, Sofie Burgos-Thorsen, Zihao Fu, Johan Irving S{\o}ltoft, Kenneth C. Enevoldsen, Chris Russell

item.title: Framing the Narrative: Ideological Mimicry in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.38256v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about politically contentious issues, yet evaluations typically treat a model's stance as a relatively stable property. Real users, however, communicate political signals through their terminology, assumptions, and personal context. We investigate whether such signals produce ideological mimicry: systematic shifts in the political stance expressed by an LLM toward the position conveyed by the interaction. If LLMs adapt their responses to these signals, they risk creating personalised political information environments in which users with opposing views receive systematically different accounts of the same issue, potentially reinforcing existing divisions. We build the Poli-SHIFT dataset and evaluation framework and assess ten LLMs across ten contentious political topics in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, systematically manipulating contested terminology, politically valenced premises, and user information, and eliciting responses in both multiple-choice and open-text formats. Across models, we find robust evidence that prompt framing shapes the political stance of LLM outputs. Substituting contested terminology while holding the substantive question fixed reverses which side of an issue a model supports in 16.9% of matched item pairs for open-weight models and 4.2% for closed-source models. Stated political ideology also systematically shifts responses toward the user's position. These findings show that political stance is not a fixed property of LLMs; the views expressed are conditional on the interaction with the user. As LLMs become increasingly personalised sources of information, such interaction-dependent adaptation could contribute to political information environments that reinforce users' existing perspectives.
item.dc:creator: Olivia Macmillan-Scott, Michael Jacobs, Nils Metternich, Mirco Musolesi

item.title: InvestigationWorlds: An Agentic Environment for Legal Investigation
item.description: arXiv:2610.04129v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce InvestigationWorlds, an agentic environment for legal investigation. We build on an underused artifact of U.S. civil litigation: the summary judgment motion. This motion relies upon a record composed of real evidence exhibits, and results in a court-adopted hypothesis that is treated as ground truth for the purposes of deciding the motion. Each environment is built from a real U.S. Federal Court case retrieved from Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER) and augmented by an attorney-validated generation pipeline that synthesizes role-tagged documents around the original record. The resulting corpus admits multiple coherent factual readings, only one of which matches the court-adopted hypothesis. Evaluating on 100 cases, we find agents often commit to incorrect hypotheses despite retrieving relevant evidence, struggling to distinguish the court-adopted hypothesis from alternative hypotheses.
item.dc:creator: Albert Yu Sun, Andrew Benard, Sil Hamilton, Anna Teresita A. Marcelo, Yong Jae Kim, Carl-Leander Henneking, Rundong Hu, Yuhong Wang, David Mimno, Bishan Yang, Igor Labutov

item.title: Preserving Orientation and Transition Order in Transition Network Analysis: A Directed Topological Proof of Concept
item.description: arXiv:2611.28249v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transition Network Analysis (TNA; tna, Nestimate) models learning as directed Markov transitions. While Nestimate also offers sequence-level higher-order models, clique-based topological tools lose directional structure: tna::cliques() returns unordered mutual subsets without homology or convergence-divergence asymmetry, and undirected persistent homology in Nestimate symmetrizes transitions into clique complexes, erasing edge orientation and triangle order. We evaluate four directed constructions on group_regulation (9 states): Dowker sink/source complexes, directed flag complexes ($dFl$), and regular GLMY path homology, compared against row-permutation and degree-preserving null models ($B = 20,000$). Across $\tau \in [0.20, 0.28]$, $\beta_1^{dFl}$ exceeds the max-symmetrized clique complex $\beta_1^{\mathrm{sym}}$ by $1$; on $\tau \in (0.239087, 0.290401]$ (e.g., $\tau = 0.26$), $\beta_1^{\mathrm{sym}} = 0$ whereas $\beta_1^{dFl} = 1$, capturing the reciprocal consensus $\leftrightarrow$ plan loop (weights $0.3958, 0.2904$). On $\tau \in (0.146825, 0.172081]$, $dFl$ also leaves the directed 3-cycle {consensus, coregulate, emotion} unfilled. Regular GLMY path homology gives $\beta_1^{\mathrm{path}} = 0$ across all thresholds (lower-tail $p = 0.012$ for its sum over $[0.14, 0.30]$ under row permutation, reflecting in-degree concentration). Dowker analysis reveals significant sink-source asymmetry: 20-21 sink vs. 0 source 2-simplices across $[0.20, 0.28]$ ($p = 0.002$ at $\tau = 0.26$), driven by six behaviors converging onto consensus ($\mathrm{InStrength} = 2.667$). Thus, directed complexes unify feedback and sink convergence over one directed graph.
item.dc:creator: Koichi Yasutake, Hitoshi Inoue

item.title: S\'anchez, Feij\'oo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
item.description: arXiv:2611.29765v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, S\'anchez, Feij\'oo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for S\'anchez and Feij\'oo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare S\'anchez and right personas spare Feij\'oo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.
item.dc:creator: V\'ictor Yeste, Candida Maria Greco, Paolo Rosso, Andrea Tagarelli
